catalog_quote: Dunan has a three-way word-tone system for simple nouns. The tone domain is not the syllable nor the mora, but the word; one of the three distinctive melodies is mapped onto the word as a whole, regardless of its length. However, the actual tone-bearing unit is the syllable. The three word-tones High, Low and Falling, are also usually called A, B and C. The High tone is characterized by a high pitch on the last syllable of the words, with all preceding syllables high, except the first one in polysyllabic words. The Low tone is evenly low throughout the word. The Falling tone is similar to the High one, but the final syllable has a falling contour if it is heavy. If the last syllable of the word is light (i.e., is a (C)V syllable), it is pronounced with a high pitch, making it indistinguishable from a High-tone word, unless it is made heavy by attaching some extra phonological material, such as the inclusive clitic =n (‘even, too’). An unrealized final fall can also trigger a downstep of the following word (Uwano 2010). ... The difference of range between the high and low pitches is usually quite small in Dunan, which makes the assessment of each word’s tonal category a difficult task. Investigation of the tone system has barely begun, and tone will thus be left unmarked in most examples. [fn. 2] All the information on tone in this chapter thus comes from Uwano (2009, 2010, 2011).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody is a lexical three-way word-tone (N-pattern accent) system: each simple noun belongs to class A/High (LH.H, final syllable high), B/Low (level low) or C/Falling (like A but with a fall on a heavy final syllable, neutralised with A on a light final syllable unless a clitic adds weight; an unrealised fall downsteps the next word). No stress is described; prominence location is not a positional stress rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress (no stress described at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Falling (C) tone is not realised on a light (C)V final syllable, making it indistinguishable from High unless e.g. inclusive =n is attached; super-heavy CVVN monosyllables are not resyllabified; some Low-tone verbs shift to Falling within their paradigm (metatony, three sub-patterns); pitch range between high and low is small; Uwano 2010 additionally notes items (mostly compounds) that fit none of the three patterns. Authors state tone is left unmarked in most examples and that all tone information comes from Uwano (2009, 2010, 2011).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word (word-tone), TBU the syllable; Uwano 2010 frames the patterns over the bunsetsu (word + enclitics), e.g. C lowers a following particle/phrase. Data are citation forms and word+clitic forms from the Sonai dialect (Uwano's speaker b. 1919).
new_statements.identity_note: Yamada, Pellard & Shimoji 2015 describe Dunan (the endonym for Yonaguni, yona1241) as a whole; their tone data come from Uwano, whose materials (2010 ff.) are from the Sonai 祖納 settlement (speaker Ikema Nae, b. 1919). Nakazawa 2023 states dialect differences between the three settlements (Sonai, Higawa, Kubura) are negligible apart from Okinawan influence in Kubura. No sub-glottocodes involved.

new_statements.translation: "For the three accent types A, B, C, which make up the three-pattern accent system, (2) is written at the end of each accent unit: (2) Type A: =, Type B: _, Type C: ]" (2014: 69). "To state the overall conclusion: it is a three-pattern accent system, but no regularity of the kind called a 'compound accent law' is found" (2014: 70). "A+A 'Aomori-ken' 'a'omori=keN= resembles the unaccented type of the Tokyo dialect. In B+A 'Yamagata-ken' jamagata_keN= the keN becomes high. In C+A 'Akita-ken' 'akita]keN= there is a half-fall before keN" (2015: 167). "In conclusion, the accent of loanwords in the Yonaguni dialect is such that type B or type C is almost predictable from the word's length and its phonotactic structure" (2016: 74).

new_statements.relation_note: Same object as the catalog's existing statement (Yamada, Pellard & Shimoji 2015: three-way word-tone system, melody mapped onto the whole word). Uwano calls it a '3型アクセント' (three-pattern accent, types A/B/C on the accent unit) rather than 'word tone', but describes the same three word-level pitch melodies and never posits stress; so the type is compatible (terminological difference only). It adds: pitch realisation of the three types, the accent-unit domain including multi-unit compounds, absence of a compound accent law, and the length/weight-based predictability of loanword class (<=3 morae C; >=4 morae B unless heavy final syllable -> C).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yonaguni (Sonai) has a three-pattern word accent system: every accent unit (a simple word, or each unit of a multi-unit compound) carries one of three pitch patterns A (=; no fall, like Tokyo unaccented), B (_; low, with a rise on a following element) or C (]; fall / half-fall at the unit end). The pattern is a property of the whole unit, not of a particular syllable, and nothing is said about stress or dynamic prominence. Loanwords: up to 3 morae take C; 4 or more morae take B unless the final syllable is heavy (ends in N or a long vowel), in which case C. Native compounds show no 'compound accent law' (the first element's class does not predict the compound's class) and productive place-name compounds usually form two or three accent units, each keeping its own pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None reported; multi-unit compounds carry one pattern per accent unit (up to three units, e.g. zjosji]taNki]daigaku_ 'women's junior college' with two falls, 2015: 168).
new_statements.exceptions: Loanword exceptions listed: zuboN_, donau_, buriKi_, razji'o_ are B although 3 morae or fewer (2014: 76); 'aribai_, dezaiN_ are B despite a heavy final syllable; korokKe] is C despite a light final (2014: 76); in Ikema Ryuichi's data 8-10 short words are B (demа, ka:do, koNbi, suki:, zuboN, cji:mu, terebi, bakecu) and karori:, patoka:, fassjoN, merodi: are B despite heavy finals; A type is rare in loanwords (only 5 sure cases, 2016: 72-73). Simple word and compound with the same first element often differ in class ('no shiki-hozon'), and A-type first elements of '-ken' are often realised as C (2015: 167).
new_statements.identity_note: All three Uwano papers describe the Sonai (祖納) variety of Yonaguni, from two speakers: Ikema Nae (b. 1919, Sonai) and, for the 2015 compound data and the 2016 loanword data, her son Ikema Ryuichi (b. 1950, Sonai). The 2016 paper reports that the two speakers agree on 13 of 14 shared loanword items. The task's citation lacked the vol. 40 pages: they are 71-105; part (3) in vol. 38 is titled 琉球与那国方言のアクセント資料（3）(without 体言), parts (4) and (5) carry 体言 in the title.

sources.note: pp. 1-3 (Sonai dialect, speaker b. 1919): the accent system is known to be a three-pattern (3型) system; 'Ａ型は下降なしの型で、文節末音節が高く終わり、続く助詞や文節を低くすることはない。Ｂ型は…極めて概略的に言えば低平調である。Ｃ型は、文節末が「軽音節」の場合はそれだけではＡ型と区別がないが、文節末が「重音節」だとその音節の中で下降調を取ってＡ型と区別される。…すなわち、Ｃ型は文節末に下降をもつ型である。' Also notes some items (esp. compounds) that do not fit the three patterns, and that the syllable (light vs heavy) plays an important role.
